clue.text: Show off horse in Arab style with even trot

definitions.note: noun sense: a person who shows off

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside the other's letters
restyling a word arranges its letters in a new fashion

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
GG, short for gee-gee, a child's word for a horse

indicators.note: even asks for the letters in the second and fourth places of the word it qualifies

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of trot

explanation.surface: A showy rider puts their horse through an Arab-style display with a steady trot.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of Arab are rearranged as BRAA, the horse goes inside to make BRAGGA, and the even letters of trot finish BRAGGART.
explanation.definitionFit: A braggart is a boastful person, someone who shows off; the clue uses the noun, as in 'he's a show-off'.

clue.text: Carefully move hands off accounts book

indicators.note: the two hands are left and right, and taking them off removes those letters

parts.note: a ledger is a book of accounts

explanation.surface: An instruction to someone handling the company accounts: keep your hands off the book.
explanation.walkthrough: Hands are L and R (left and right); removing both from LEDGER leaves EDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To edge is to inch forward cautiously, a direct synonym for moving carefully.

clue.text: Fox comes to grief at last in tortuous fable

indicators.note: something tortuous is twisted, so the letters are twisted out of order
at last points to the final letter of the word before it

parts.note: last letter of grief
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fox meets a sticky end in a convoluted fable, like one of Aesop's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fox' looks like the animal of the fable, but it is the verb meaning to puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: To fox someone is to puzzle or confuse them, a synonym of the verb baffle.

clue.text: Sweet cake discovered during summer in Guernsey

indicators.note: something discovered during a stretch of words is found lying inside them

parts.note: the run of letters straddling these three words

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker found a lovely pastry during a summer break on Guernsey.
explanation.walkthrough: Guernsey is one of the Channel Islands; the letters sit across summER IN GUErnsey.
explanation.definitionFit: A meringue is a light confection of whipped egg white and sugar, baked as a small sweet cake.

clue.text: Nick subtly hit on lady taking away her heart by cunning

parts.note: to nick is British slang for to steal

indicators.note: doing something subtly suggests a sly rearrangement of the word that follows
removing the heart of a word drops its middle letters

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, losing its middle pair

explanation.surface: A smooth operator, Nick, makes a subtle pass at a woman and steals her heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a man's name but is the verb to steal. LADY without its heart AD leaves LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealthily means in a sly, furtive way, so doing something by cunning is an adverbial equivalent.

clue.text: Friend eats the Spanish top class dish

indicators.note: a word that eats another takes it inside itself

parts.note: a pal is a friend
el is Spanish for the
A is the top grade or class

explanation.surface: A pal tucks into a first-rate Spanish meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top class' is a common crossword stand-in for A, as in an A grade or A-list.
explanation.definitionFit: Paella is a Spanish rice dish cooked with saffron, seafood or meat in a wide shallow pan.

clue.text: Woman with degree from commercial university's got into great career

definitions.note: the answer covers anyone with a degree; woman narrows it for the surface

indicators.note: to career is to rush wildly about, so the word beside it is thrown out of order
getting into something means going inside it

parts.note: the letters of great rearranged
an ad is a commercial
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A woman holding a business degree has gone on to a brilliant career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' looks like the noun but works as the verb meaning to hurtle about, so it signals the jumbling of great.
explanation.definitionFit: A graduate is a person who has completed a university degree course.

clue.text: Cock up with business trip

parts.note: to cock up is to blunder, to err
and means together with

explanation.surface: Something went badly wrong on a work trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Business trip' reads as a corporate jaunt, but here business means a task.
explanation.definitionFit: An errand is a short trip made to carry out a small piece of business, such as collecting something.

clue.text: Lure of revolutionary lover tailed off

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the word is read backwards
a word tailed off has lost its final letter

parts.note: a partner is a lover

explanation.surface: The romantic pull of a radical lover whose passion fizzled out.
explanation.walkthrough: PARTNER loses its last letter to become PARTNE, which read backwards is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To lure someone is to tempt them into a trap, which is what entrapping them means.

clue.text: Gape at own goal by the French

parts.note: OG is the standard abbreviation for own goal in football
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A football fan stares in disbelief at an own goal scored by the French side.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to stare at someone openly, so gaping at them is a near synonym.

clue.text: Can be excused for housing four in part of roof

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a structure housing something holds it inside

parts.note: a gable is the triangular end section of a pitched roof
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Some roofing defect might be pardoned, or an excuse is offered for a fault in the roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' in the clue is not a link word here: it is taken literally and goes at the front of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forgivable is pardonable, able to be excused; the definition is a phrase standing in for the adjective.

clue.text: One bumped into by man with butty?

definitions.meaning: a jokey reading: to barge is to bump into, and like employee, the -ee suffix names the one it is done to
a narrowboat worker; a butty is an unpowered canal boat towed behind a motor boat

explanation.surface: Who gets jostled in a crowd? A chap clutching his sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a butty is also a sandwich, which is the picture the surface paints; on the canals it is a towed boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargee is a person who works on a canal barge, often handling a towed butty boat alongside the motor boat.

clue.text: Hurry up vote on mega-redevelopment

indicators.note: redevelopment rebuilds something in a new form, so the letters are rebuilt

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Residents are urged to cast their ballots quickly on a huge building scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: Get a move on is an informal idiom urging someone to go faster, the same command as hurry up.

clue.text: Close deal in return for final drink

parts.note: nigh means near or close

indicators.note: something in return comes back the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a pact is a deal or agreement

explanation.surface: Sealing a business deal and getting one last round in exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close deal' looks like one phrase about finishing negotiations, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightcap is the last drink of the evening, typically taken just before going to bed.

clue.text: Way to take on extreme speech impediment

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
utter means complete or extreme

explanation.surface: A method for tackling a severe problem with talking.
explanation.definitionFit: A stutter is a speech disorder in which sounds are involuntarily repeated or prolonged.

clue.text: Hugeness of God doesn't begin to comprehend usual way of things

indicators.note: to comprehend is literally to grasp or enclose, holding something inside
a word that does not begin has lost its opening letter

parts.note: a deity is a god
the norm is the usual pattern

explanation.surface: A theological musing that the vastness of God is beyond understanding the ordinary world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doesn't begin' applies to the word for God, which loses its first letter before wrapping round the usual way of things.
explanation.definitionFit: Enormity is often used for great size or immensity, though purists keep it for great wickedness.

clue.text: Speciality food shop has extremely short supply

indicators.note: falling short means missing the final letter

parts.note: a deli (delicatessen) sells speciality foods
very means extremely

explanation.surface: A delicatessen is running seriously low on stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short supply' wants to be a phrase meaning scarcity; short actually trims VERY to VER.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver is to bring or hand over goods, which is to supply them.

clue.text: Very happy to mention review about Wicked cast

indicators.note: to review is to look back, so the word is read backwards
about means going around, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: to cite is to mention

indicators.note: wicked as in naughty or unruly, so the letters misbehave and move out of order

parts.note: the letters of cast rearranged

explanation.surface: A theatre fan is thrilled to bring up a glowing review of the cast of the musical Wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: Wicked is a hit stage musical, which hides that the word here signals an anagram. ETIC wraps round the rearranged cast after its E.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstatic means overwhelmingly joyful, an intensified synonym of very happy.

clue.text: Northern side of church's poorly lit by candles, primarily

indicators.note: something poorly is unwell and out of sorts, so its letters are disordered

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
the letters of lit rearranged

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letter of the word before it

parts.note: first letter of candles

explanation.surface: The north aisle of a church is gloomy, lit only by candlelight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Northern side of church' wants to be the north transept; the definition is a football team. Celtic is a Glasgow club, a side in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Celtic is a Scottish football club based in Glasgow, so a team, or side, from the north of Britain.

clue.text: Flower border described by piece of writing

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to trace round it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: prose is ordinary written language
a rim is a border or edge

explanation.surface: A garden writer describes the flowers in a herbaceous border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower border' reads as a garden bed; flower is the definition and border a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The primrose is a pale yellow wild flower that blooms in early spring.

clue.text: Sorry about constant time taken off with awful flu

indicators.note: something awful is a mess, so the letters are jumbled
time taken off means the letter for time is removed

parts.note: true means faithful, constant
the letters of flu rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is apologetic about missing work for ages with a dreadful bout of flu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constant time' looks like a phrase meaning always; constant is TRUE and time is the T removed from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rueful means regretful, expressing sorrow, so it fits sorry in the sense of feeling remorse.

clue.text: Most timid model pursues quiet approval

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
yes signals approval
T as in the Model T Ford

explanation.surface: A very bashful fashion model seeks a quiet word of approval.
explanation.walkthrough: Pursues means comes after, so the model's T goes last. The Model T was an early Ford car.
explanation.definitionFit: Shyest is the superlative of shy, meaning the most timid or bashful.

clue.text: Only one by heartless man's grave

indicators.note: a heartless word has had its central letter removed

parts.note: sole means the only one
taken as written, losing its middle

explanation.surface: A lonely churchyard: just one person standing beside a cold man's tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' looks like a noun for a burial place; it is the adjective meaning serious.
explanation.definitionFit: Solemn and grave are synonyms as adjectives, both meaning serious and dignified in manner.

clue.text: AC/DC lead, for example?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Australian hard rock band, an example of a loud guitar music genre
second meaning: lead is a dense element, one of a class of dense metallic elements

explanation.walkthrough: AC/DC looks like electrical current and lead like a cable, so the clue pretends to be about wiring; both are examples, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy metal is both a loud rock genre that AC/DC exemplify and the chemical class of dense metals such as lead.

clue.text: Joke heard from Cockney: "Where do h'acorns come from?"

indicators.note: something heard in a Cockney accent goes by its sound as that speaker says it, not by spelling

parts.note: acorns grow on oaks, and this speaker adds a stray h

explanation.surface: A music-hall gag in a Cockney accent with a riddle about acorns.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys stereotypically drop their h's; this one overcorrects, putting h before vowels, so oaks comes out with an h. The quote's own h'acorns signals the habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoax is a trick or practical joke meant to deceive someone.

clue.text: Most of orchestra's in concert room

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its last letter

parts.note: Manchester's famous symphony orchestra, named after its German-born founder Sir Charles

explanation.surface: Nearly all the orchestra members are sitting in the auditorium.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hallé is Manchester's symphony orchestra; dropping its final E leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hall, as in concert hall, is a large room or building where performances are held.

clue.text: Cancel rugby union match

parts.note: RU is the abbreviation for rugby union
a bout is a contest or match, as in boxing

explanation.surface: An order to call off a rugby game.
explanation.definitionFit: To rub out is to erase, so it means to cancel something written; it is also slang for to kill.

clue.text: Grumble about order given without any fuss

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
the OM, Order of Merit, is a British honour bestowed on a few
plain means simple, unadorned

explanation.surface: Someone moans about an instruction being issued with no explanation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order given' reads as a command; it is an honour that is awarded, the Order of Merit.
explanation.definitionFit: To complain is to express dissatisfaction, which is what a grumble does; both are verbs here.
